jQuery is a Javascript file that allows written Javascript to be much more cross browser compatible using a short hand system. In the old days of Javascript, you'd first have to sniff out the browser version, now you can just start writing jQuery without all the browser sniffing.

Node.js is a new server side (as opposed to client side) programming language that uses the same Javascript people are already familiar with. I haven't used it myself, the concept is quite interesting and a great way for new programmers to have to only learn one language instead of multiple. So it's popularity is on the rise.

Analytics and ads are how websites owners determine who, how many, how often people use a website and view ads. Websites still cost money to run and a lot of website creators like to know this information.

To those really interested. jQuery is older than dirt now. I don't know anyone still using it. Though obviously JavaScript is still used heavily (it's just different frameworks/libraries).

It seems to be the most popular of the short hand Javascript methods. jQuery is nothing more than a Javascript file referenced before the rest of your code is loaded. It's a series of checks and balances to make sure that your code is as compatible as possible with every browser. The actual file is usually pulled from a shared hosted resource, that way if your website visitor has been to any other website pulling that same file, it may already be cached by that persons browser and wouldn't need to be downloaded again.

I see it as not having to reinvent the wheel. There are simply to many platforms and browsers to constantly write functions to adjust your script to each and every possible combination and the anomalies that come with it. Chrome on Chromebooks, Chrome on Apple, Safari on Windows, Opera on Android, Konqueror on Windows.

I've found other tasks which are easier (at least for me) using jQuery. I needed to create a website that didn't store anything in cache so the user couldn't use the back button as there would be no history. The website wasn't for public use and stored sensitive data. The ideal was that if a person perusing sensitive data gets up from their workstation and walks away, another person can't sit down at their workstation and start hitting the back button to see what they were looking at. They would be able to see only the most current page they were on. I used jQuery to load the page frame with menu and so forth and then only the content in the center changed as they moved around the website and I simply stored a cookie with their location, so if they logged out, they could return to the exact spot, even though the URL never changed on the website. jQuery worked really well in this situation, specially since I sometimes modified sections of sections and things would get up to 5 layers deep.

I don't work for jQuery and could give a shit what or how people do things, but for me personally, I'm glad I took the time to learn it as even though some of my websites are pretty complicated, I rarely ever get calls about browser incompatibility.

P.S. For anyone reading this, I know there is multiple no-cache options that can be implemented, but some browsers and operating systems simply ignore them, I'm looking at you Chrome on Chrome OS, and so that's why I used the nuclear option of eliminating the practical use of the back button.
